practices.title: Breathing Tide
practices.desc: Follow a soft, expanding light. Let the next breath arrive gently.
practices.instruction: Let the light grow as you breathe in, and soften as you breathe out. Stay with a comfortable, unforced breath.
practices.safety: No breath holding. The timing is optional: breathe naturally or stop if the pace feels uncomfortable or you feel dizzy.

phases.title: Breathe in
phases.cue: Gently, and only as far as feels comfortable.

phases.title: Breathe out
phases.cue: Gently, and only as far as feels comfortable.

practices.title: Box Breathing
practices.desc: Trace a steady square, one phase at a time. Holds are optional.
practices.instruction: Follow the light around the square. Each side marks a phase. You can turn holds off and breathe continuously.
practices.safety: Never strain or force a breath hold. Choose “No holds” if holding is uncomfortable. If unsure about breath holds because of a health condition, seek advice from your clinician.

phases.title: Breathe in
phases.cue: Gently, and only as far as feels comfortable.

phases.title: Hold gently
phases.cue: Only if comfortable. No strain, no forcing.

phases.title: Breathe out
phases.cue: Gently, and only as far as feels comfortable.

phases.title: Rest gently
phases.cue: Only if comfortable. No strain, no forcing.

practices.title: Here & Now
practices.desc: Reconnect with your surroundings through five simple senses.
practices.instruction: Notice things in your actual surroundings, not just on this screen. Tap a stone for each thing you notice. No writing or sharing needed.
practices.safety: Keep your eyes open if that feels safer. Skip or substitute any sense that is inaccessible, unpleasant, or uncomfortable. Nothing needs to be tasted or touched.

steps.title: See
steps.line: Notice five things you can see.
steps.hint: A color, a shape, the way light meets a surface.

steps.title: Feel
steps.hint: Your feet supported, the chair, your sleeve. No need to touch new objects.

steps.title: Hear
steps.hint: Nearby or far away. If hearing is not accessible, notice three visual details.

steps.title: Smell
steps.line: Notice two neutral or pleasant smells.
steps.hint: If none are available, recall familiar scents or choose two colors instead.

steps.title: Taste
steps.hint: Nothing needs to go in your mouth. Alternatively, name one thing you appreciate.

practices.title: Soften & Release
practices.desc: Notice gentle tension and release, with a moving body guide.
practices.instruction: The highlighted area shows where to place your attention. Use only light tension, breathe normally, and notice the release. The final step is rest only.
practices.safety: Avoid tensing painful or injured areas; choose “Relax only” or skip. Stop if you feel pain or discomfort. This is a short PMR-inspired adaptation, not a clinical protocol.

phases.title: Hands
phases.effortCue: Lightly close your hands. Keep breathing normally.
phases.releaseCue: Let your fingers soften. Notice without judging.

phases.title: Shoulders
phases.effortCue: Lift your shoulders just a little. Keep breathing.
phases.releaseCue: Let your shoulders settle. There is no perfect position.

phases.title: Feet
phases.effortCue: Lightly press your feet into the floor. No straining.
phases.releaseCue: Release the effort in your feet and lower legs.

phases.title: Rest & notice
phases.releaseCue: Let your whole body be supported. Breathe naturally.

practices.title: The Seated Reset
practices.desc: Ease your shoulders, uncurl your hands, and gently turn your head.
practices.intro: Move a little. Notice a little.
practices.instruction: Sit on a stable, non-wheeled chair, with feet supported. Use a small comfortable range. The figure is a schematic cue, not a posture assessment.
practices.safety: Skip any movement that is unsuitable, painful, or makes you dizzy. Do not force a stretch or roll your neck. Check with a clinician if unsure whether these movements are suitable.

phases.title: Shoulder lift & release
phases.cue: Gently lift your shoulders a little, then let them lower.

phases.title: Open & soften hands
phases.cue: Slowly uncurl your fingers, then let your hands soften.

phases.title: Gentle neck turns
phases.cue: Turn left within a comfortable range, return to center, then right.

practices.title: Body Scan Journey
practices.desc: Move attention gently through supported body areas.
steps: Feet & support
Notice contact with the floor or chair. Nothing needs to change.
Legs
Notice whatever is present, or choose to focus on the room instead.
Hands
Notice the weight and temperature of your hands.
Shoulders
Notice support. There is no need to soften on command.
Face
Notice your expression without judging it.
Whole body
Broaden attention, then look around the room.
practices.safety: Skip any area or use external focus if body attention feels uncomfortable.
practices.instruction: Notice contact with the floor or chair. Nothing needs to change.

practices.title: Full Muscle Release
practices.desc: Explore light effort and release across several areas.
steps: Hands
Optional: close your hands lightly, then let them open.
Arms
Optional: use a little effort in the arms, then release.
Shoulders
Optional: make a small lift, then return comfortably.
Feet
Optional: press feet lightly into support, then release.
Rest
No effort here. Notice the chair supporting you.
practices.safety: Use only light effort. Avoid painful or injured areas. Relax-only mode is available.
practices.instruction: Optional: close your hands lightly, then let them open.

practices.title: Hand & Finger Reset
practices.desc: A close-up guide to gently opening and resting your hands.
steps: Settle
Rest your forearms comfortably. Keep wrists neutral.
Open gently
Gently uncurl your fingers in a comfortable range.
Return
Return to a relaxed hand. Do not grip tightly.
Rest
Let the hands be supported.
practices.safety: Stop for pain, tingling, or discomfort. This is a movement cue, not treatment.
practices.instruction: Rest your forearms comfortably. Keep wrists neutral.

practices.title: Shoulder Reset
practices.desc: Follow a small lift and a gentle return to rest.
steps: Settle
Sit supported with arms resting comfortably.
Small lift
If comfortable, lift shoulders a little. Keep breathing naturally.
Return
Return gently. Avoid forcing shoulders downward.
Rest
Notice support and stop whenever you prefer.
practices.safety: Use a small comfortable range. Skip painful or injured areas.
practices.instruction: Sit supported with arms resting comfortably.

practices.title: Seated Foot & Ankle Movement
practices.desc: Explore a small up-and-down movement while seated.
steps: Settle
Use a stable chair. Support your leg and foot comfortably.
Small movement
If comfortable, move the ankle gently up and down.
Other side
Repeat on the other side only if suitable.
Rest
Return both feet to comfortable support.
practices.safety: Do not force range. Skip if movement is unsuitable, painful, or causes discomfort.
practices.instruction: Use a stable chair. Support your leg and foot comfortably.

practices.title: Mindful Listening
practices.desc: Notice nearby and distant sounds without recording them.
steps: Arrive
Look around. Choose a comfortable position.
Nearby
Notice a nearby sound, or a nearby visual detail.
Further away
Notice something further away. No need to search hard.
Whole space
Allow attention to include the room as a whole.
practices.safety: Use visual details if hearing is inaccessible or focusing on sound is uncomfortable. No microphone is used.
practices.instruction: Look around. Choose a comfortable position.

practices.title: Three-Minute Pause
practices.desc: Notice, choose an anchor, then broaden awareness.
steps: Notice
Notice how you are arriving: thoughts, feelings, or surroundings.
Anchor
Choose natural breathing, supported feet, or a visual detail.
Broaden
Include the body and room. Choose one useful next step.
practices.safety: Breathing is optional. Keep attention external if that feels more comfortable.
practices.instruction: Notice how you are arriving: thoughts, feelings, or surroundings.

practices.title: Quiet Place Visualization
practices.desc: Explore a gentle imagined scene, with motion optional.
steps: Choose
Choose an ordinary place that feels comfortable enough.
Notice
Notice imagined light, colors, or textures. You can simply view the photograph.
Stay gently
No need to create a vivid image. Keep your eyes open if preferred.
Return
Look around your actual room and notice its support.
practices.safety: Skip imagery if it feels uncomfortable. Choose grounding in your actual surroundings instead.
practices.instruction: Choose an ordinary place that feels comfortable enough.

practices.title: Slow Walking Awareness
practices.desc: A preview of slow steps, followed by screen-away prompts.
steps: Prepare
Choose a clear, level space. Preview while stationary.
Step
Put the screen away before moving. Walk at your own comfortable pace.
Notice
Notice ordinary contact and surroundings, without changing your gait.
Return
Stop in a stable position and return attention to the room.
practices.safety: Use only if walking is suitable. Do not watch or operate the screen while walking. Seated awareness is an alternative.
practices.instruction: Choose a clear, level space. Preview while stationary.

practices.title: Evening Wind-Down
practices.desc: A quiet sequence of support, awareness, and optional release.
steps: Supported rest
Choose a comfortable supported position.
Notice support
Notice the surface supporting you, without trying to sleep.
Gentle release
Let hands and shoulders rest. Tensing is not required.
Set down
Notice one thing that can wait until tomorrow.
Finish
End here or continue resting. There is no outcome to achieve.
practices.safety: This practice does not treat sleep difficulties or guarantee sleep. Stop or adapt if uncomfortable.

resources.label: MINDFUL MOMENT
resources.title: A little pause. A fresh perspective.
resources.desc: A gentle, guided breathing space between appointments.
resources.body: A brief pause is not another thing to achieve. It is a chance to notice how you are arriving in this moment.
steps: Settle into a supported position. Keep your eyes open or softly lower your gaze.
Breathe gently in for four seconds, then out for six. Do not force or hold your breath.
When your attention wanders, return to the feeling of your feet on the ground.
resources.extra: If focusing on your breath is uncomfortable, breathe normally and name five things you can see instead. Stop if you feel dizzy or distressed.

resources.label: PRACTITIONER CARE
resources.title: Caring without carrying it all
resources.desc: A compassionate approach to boundaries and recovery.
resources.body: Caring deeply and protecting your own capacity can coexist. A boundary is not a measure of how much you care; it is a way to make care sustainable.
steps: Notice your early signs of depletion: irritability, emotional distance, or difficulty switching off. These experiences deserve attention, not self-judgment.
Create a closing ritual: finish essential documentation, identify the next safe step, and name what can wait.
Use supervision and peer support. Keep patient information within approved confidential settings.
If distress persists or affects safe practice, seek support from an occupational health service or qualified mental health professional.
resources.extra: Reflection: What is one responsibility you can share, clarify, or set down today?

resources.label: IN YOUR TOOLKIT
resources.title: Finding your feet in the present
resources.desc: An adaptable sensory grounding exercise for shared practice.
resources.body: Grounding may help some people reconnect with the present. Offer it as an invitation rather than a requirement, and ask what feels accessible and comfortable.
steps: Look around and gently name five things you can see.
Notice four physical sensations, such as the chair supporting you or your feet on the floor.
Listen for three sounds; then notice two neutral or pleasant smells, if comfortable.
Name one thing that feels steady right now. Skip any sense that is inaccessible or uncomfortable.
resources.extra: This practice is optional and is not a treatment or crisis intervention. Stop or adapt it if it increases discomfort.

resources.label: REST & RECOVERY
resources.title: Make room for restorative rest
resources.desc: Small, realistic changes that can support a steadier sleep routine.
resources.body: Rest is personal. Begin with curiosity about routines, responsibilities, symptoms, medication, and the environment rather than assuming there is one perfect schedule.
steps: Choose a realistic, reasonably consistent wake-up time.
Make a small transition between the demands of the day and bedtime.
Discuss the timing of caffeine and other stimulants with an appropriate professional.
For persistent sleep difficulties, consider assessment and evidence-based support such as CBT-I.
resources.extra: Avoid making changes to prescribed medication without consulting the prescriber.

resources.label: REFLECTIVE PRACTICE
resources.title: Leave the day a little lighter
resources.desc: A brief end-of-day reflection without judgment.
resources.body: Reflection is most useful when it creates understanding rather than another standard to meet. You do not need to solve the whole day before you leave it.
steps: Name one moment of connection or meaningful work.
Notice one demand that felt difficult. Describe it without blaming yourself.
Choose one practical support for tomorrow: a pause, a conversation, or a clearer boundary.
resources.extra: Keep personal reflections free of patient names or identifying details.

resources.label: MEASUREMENT & CARE
resources.title: A score is a starting point
resources.desc: Using well-being measures to support, not replace, conversation.
resources.body: Patient-reported measures add one perspective to care. Scores should be interpreted alongside the person’s own account, functioning, context, preferences, and a clinical assessment.
steps: Explain why you are using a measure, its recall period, and how the information will be used.
Review change with the person. Ask what fits their experience and what does not.
Discuss missing responses without treating them as a risk signal on their own.
Do not infer a diagnosis or safety status from a well-being score. Use your service’s assessment and escalation protocols.
resources.extra: This demonstration displays synthetic WHO-5-style totals on a 0–100 scale. It does not administer, validate, or interpret a clinical questionnaire.

resources.label: ASKING FOR SUPPORT
resources.title: Start a useful support conversation
resources.desc: Turn a difficult demand into a clear request.
resources.body: A useful support conversation describes the situation and the help needed. You do not need to wait until you are overwhelmed to ask.
steps: Describe the demand: "I have several time-critical tasks and need help prioritizing."
Explain the practical impact without sharing patient details in this app.
Make one specific request: help with a task, protected time, clarification, or a short conversation.
Agree who will do what, and when you will check back. Use your workplace escalation pathway for immediate safety concerns.
resources.extra: Practice wording: "Can we agree the immediate priorities and who can help?" This is an educational conversation guide.

resources.label: AFTER YOUR SHIFT
resources.title: A gentler transition home
resources.desc: Close the workday with a realistic transition.
resources.body: A transition does not need to erase the day. It can help you acknowledge what happened and move into the next part of your life.
steps: Complete essential handover and documentation in your approved workplace system.
Identify one unfinished matter and its agreed next owner or next step.
Choose a small transition: change clothes, have a drink, sit quietly, or take a comfortable walk.
Ask yourself what recovery is realistic today. If the shift remains difficult to process, consider a trusted colleague or professional support.
resources.extra: Original Serein reflection: "A difficult shift does not erase the care you gave."

resources.title: A boundary you can actually say
resources.label: BOUNDARIES
resources.body: A useful boundary explains your capacity and offers a workable next step. Adapt the words to your role and workplace responsibilities.
steps: Name the request or demand clearly.
Describe your current capacity: "I can complete this after the urgent task, or we can agree another owner."
Offer a realistic option rather than promising work you cannot safely complete.
Confirm priorities with the appropriate supervisor when competing demands affect safe care.
resources.extra: Try: "I want to help. Can we agree what should take priority and what can wait?"

resources.title: Check in with a colleague
resources.label: PEER CONNECTION
resources.desc: Offer connection without pushing for disclosure.
resources.body: A supportive check-in can be short and respectful. Let the colleague choose whether to talk.
steps: Ask permission: "Would a quick check-in be useful?"
Offer a choice: listen, practical help, or a quiet break.
Listen without diagnosing, minimizing, or insisting on details.
Respect privacy and workplace safeguarding responsibilities. Help the person access appropriate support when needed.
resources.extra: Try: "Would you like me to listen, help with something practical, or give you some space?"

resources.title: When everything feels urgent
resources.label: WORKLOAD CLARITY
resources.desc: Turn competing demands into a shared decision.
resources.body: Use a brief conversation to clarify priorities and available help. Clinical urgency belongs within your professional assessment and local protocols.
steps: List the competing tasks in your approved work environment. Do not enter patient information here.
Identify immediate safety concerns and escalate through your workplace process.
Ask the appropriate lead to agree the order and who can help.
Repeat the agreement back and arrange a check-back if circumstances change.
resources.extra: Try: "These tasks overlap. Can we confirm the immediate priorities and available support?"

resources.title: Prepare for a difficult conversation
resources.label: CLEAR COMMUNICATION
resources.desc: Use observations, impact, and a clear request.
resources.body: Preparation can make a conversation more specific. Choose an appropriate private setting and follow your workplace policy.
steps: Describe an observable event rather than a personal label.
Explain the impact on work or your ability to contribute.
Ask an open question and allow the other person to respond.
Agree one practical next step, an owner, and a review time.
resources.extra: Practice: "When the plan changed without a handover, I was unsure of my next task. How can we make the next change clearer?"

resources.title: Notice a small moment of meaning
resources.label: REFLECTION
resources.desc: Reflect without turning the day into a grade.
resources.body: A reflection can acknowledge care, learning, or connection. A difficult day can remain difficult even when something meaningful happened.
steps: Recall one ordinary moment you want to acknowledge.
Name what mattered: kindness, teamwork, asking a question, or noticing a need.
Describe it without patient names or identifying details.
Let it be enough. You do not have to find a positive lesson in every experience.
resources.extra: Prompt: "One moment I want to acknowledge today is..."

resources.title: A supportive team conversation
resources.label: FOR TEAM LEADERS
resources.desc: Move from encouragement to practical support.
resources.body: A useful team conversation asks about working conditions and follows through on what can change. This is an educational conversation template.
steps: Ask what is making the work harder and what is already helping.
Clarify practical barriers such as workload, breaks, role clarity, or access to supervision.
Agree one feasible change and an accountable owner.
Check back. Do not ask staff to disclose private health information in a group.
resources.extra: Try: "What would make this shift more workable, and what can we change together?"

reflections.text: You can care deeply without carrying everything alone.
A difficult shift does not erase the care you gave.
You are allowed to ask for support before you reach your limit.
One small pause can make room for the next safe step.
Reflection is a place to understand yourself, not grade yourself.
Some days, recovery begins with doing one thing less.
Your needs belong in the conversation, too.
Rest is part of a sustainable practice.

[3] NHS inform · Grounding exercises ↗ The 5–4–3–2–1 sensory sequence, with optional accessibility substitutions here.
[4] Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital · Relaxation techniques ↗ Progressive muscle relaxation background. The shortened routine and relax-only option here are adaptations.
[5] NHS · Sitting exercises ↗ Stable seating and comfortable neck-turning guidance. The combined 90-second seated reset is a Serein adaptation.
[6] Calm · Box breathing ↗ Four-phase square breathing; holds are optional in this interface.

hands.title: Hands & fingers
hands.alt: AI-generated reference of two open hands resting palm-up on the lap.
cues: Support your hands on your lap. Palms can rest in a comfortable position.
Use only a light curl; then let the fingers uncurl without forcing them straight.
Do not squeeze hard or copy a range that feels uncomfortable.
hands.photo: A relaxed, open-hand position. The photo is not a target for finger extension.

shoulders.title: Shoulders & neck
shoulders.alt: AI-generated close-up of level, relaxed shoulders and a neutral neck.
cues: Let your head stay comfortably centered. Keep breathing normally.
Lift your shoulders only a little, then let them settle naturally.
Avoid pulling the shoulders forcefully down or holding your breath.
shoulders.photo: Shoulders at rest. Notice a comfortable head position, not a rigid posture target.

feet.title: Feet & support
feet.alt: AI-generated reference of both feet supported flat on the floor in a stable chair.
cues: Keep the whole foot supported. Use an appropriate foot support if needed.
If comfortable, press very lightly into the support without lifting the heel or curling the toes.
Let the effort go. Skip if painful or unsuitable.
feet.photo: Both feet remain supported. Pressing is gentle effort, not a visible ankle stretch.

neck.title: A gentle head turn
neck.alt: AI-generated reference of a seated adult making a small horizontal head turn with level shoulders.
cues: Keep shoulders comfortable and facing forward. Let your chin stay level.
Turn a little toward your own left, return to center, then gently toward your right.
Use a comfortable range; no neck rolling, stretching forcefully, or matching a target angle.
neck.photo: One example of a small head turn. Your comfortable range may be smaller.

rest.title: Rest & notice
rest.alt: AI-generated reference of a comfortable neutral neck and relaxed shoulders.
cues: Let your body be supported by the chair and the floor.
Allow hands, shoulders, and feet to settle. There is no more tensing in this step.
Breathe naturally and notice what is present, without needing it to change.
rest.photo: A quiet resting position. This image is illustrative, not a posture assessment.

sensoryExamples.name: A patch of light
sensoryExamples.hint: Notice where daylight or a lamp falls on a real surface near you.

sensoryExamples.name: A nearby color
sensoryExamples.hint: Let your eyes find one color in the room. What shade is it?

sensoryExamples.name: A familiar shape
sensoryExamples.hint: Perhaps the edge of a window, a book, or another object already nearby.

sensoryExamples.name: A gentle shadow
sensoryExamples.hint: Look for a shadow or a change in brightness in your actual surroundings.

sensoryExamples.name: A small detail
sensoryExamples.hint: Notice a line, a pattern, or a texture you can see. Nothing special is required.

sensoryExamples.name: Feet supported
sensoryExamples.hint: Notice the support under your feet, without pressing harder.

sensoryExamples.name: The chair beneath you
sensoryExamples.hint: If comfortable, notice how your seat is supporting your weight.

sensoryExamples.name: Your sleeve
sensoryExamples.hint: Notice the fabric already touching your skin. You do not need to touch a new object.

sensoryExamples.name: Air on your skin
sensoryExamples.hint: If comfortable, notice the temperature of the air on your hands or face.

sensoryExamples.name: Hands at rest
sensoryExamples.hint: Notice where your hands are supported. Choose a different sensation if needed.

sensoryExamples.name: A distant sound
sensoryExamples.hint: Listen for a sound further away. If hearing is inaccessible, notice a distant visual detail.

sensoryExamples.name: A nearby hum
sensoryExamples.hint: Perhaps a fan or appliance is audible. It is okay if there is no hum.

sensoryExamples.name: A soft rustle
sensoryExamples.hint: Notice an existing sound of fabric, paper, or leaves. No need to create one.

sensoryExamples.name: A passing voice
sensoryExamples.hint: If a comfortable voice is already nearby, notice its sound without needing to follow it.

sensoryExamples.name: Something quieter
sensoryExamples.hint: See if a quieter sound is present. Silence is okay; you can choose another sense.

sensoryExamples.name: Fresh air
sensoryExamples.hint: If a neutral outdoor scent is already available, notice it. No need to go anywhere.

sensoryExamples.name: A familiar scent
sensoryExamples.hint: A gentle remembered scent is an option when no comfortable smell is available.

sensoryExamples.name: A drink nearby
sensoryExamples.hint: Only if a familiar drink is already there and its scent is pleasant to you.

sensoryExamples.name: Something neutral
sensoryExamples.hint: You can choose an ordinary neutral smell. Avoid seeking out strong scents.

sensoryExamples.name: Or two colors
sensoryExamples.hint: If smell is uncomfortable or inaccessible, notice two colors instead.

sensoryExamples.name: A taste already there
sensoryExamples.hint: Only notice an existing taste if comfortable. You do not need to eat or drink anything.

sensoryExamples.name: A remembered flavor
sensoryExamples.hint: If helpful, recall a familiar pleasant flavor. You can skip this sense altogether.

sensoryExamples.name: Or one appreciation
sensoryExamples.hint: Instead of taste, name one ordinary thing you appreciate in this moment.

sensoryExamples.name: Something steady
sensoryExamples.hint: Another option: notice one source of support, such as the chair or a trusted person.

sensoryExamples.name: Simply skip
sensoryExamples.hint: Skipping is always an option. Use the Skip step button whenever you prefer.
